questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: Identify the central claim of a design brief
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief opens with a sentence about load capacity, then lists materials and deadlines; which sentence states the main idea?

options.text: The sentence about load capacity, since all other points serve it.
The sentence about materials, because materials dominate the brief.
options.misconception: confuses a supporting detail with the central claim

options.text: The sentence about load capacity, because it frames every later requirement.
options.misconception: mistakes the first sentence for the main idea

options.text: The deadline sentence, because schedules drive engineering work.
options.misconception: treats a logistical constraint as the purpose

questions.explanation: The main idea is the claim the rest of the brief supports; materials and deadlines are constraints, not the purpose. The tempting first-sentence reading fails when the first sentence is only context.
questions.hint: Ask which point the others exist to serve.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: Locate a specific stated requirement in a brief

stimulus.body: The bracket must hold 200 kilograms without deformation. Finish is matte black. Delivery is due in six weeks.

questions.stem: According to the engineer's design brief, what finish is required for the bracket?

options.text: Gloss white, because finishes are usually bright.
options.misconception: invents a finish not stated in the brief

options.text: Matte black, as the brief specifies.
Bare metal, to save on coating cost.
options.misconception: substitutes a cost-saving assumption for the stated finish

options.text: Anodized silver, matching common hardware.
options.misconception: imports a default finish from outside the brief

questions.explanation: The brief states the finish directly as matte black. The other options add outside assumptions about cost or convention that the brief never mentions.
questions.hint: Scan the brief for the finish word.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: Recognize the tone of a design brief
questions.stem: An engineer's brief says 'The housing shall not exceed 30 mm, period.' What tone does that sentence set, and how do you know?

answer.exemplar: The tone is firm and non-negotiable, signaled by 'shall not' and the emphatic 'period,' which closes debate. A softer brief would use 'should' or 'ideally.'

questions.explanation: Modal 'shall not' plus the emphatic closer mark a hard requirement rather than a preference. The tempting reading of mere emphasis misses the contractual force of 'shall.'
questions.hint: Look at the modal verb and the closing word.

options.text: The joint is heavier than planned.

options.text: The joint failed a 500-cycle fatigue test.

questions.explanation: An 'unacceptable' attitude needs hard evidence of failure; a fatigue-test failure supplies it. Appearance, weight, or common parts do not establish unacceptability.
questions.hint: Pick evidence that directly shows failure, not opinion.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: Name the rhetorical move in a brief

stimulus.body: The original spec allowed 5 mm tolerance. Field data shows 2 mm is achievable. Therefore the spec should tighten to 2 mm.

questions.stem: What move does the engineer's argument make?

options.text: It generalizes from one field site to all sites.
options.misconception: misreads a scope claim as a generalization

options.text: It rejects the original spec entirely.
options.misconception: overstates a tightening as a rejection

options.text: It revises a requirement downward using new evidence.
It blames the original designer for error.
options.misconception: reads a neutral revision as an accusation

questions.explanation: The argument keeps the spec but tightens tolerance based on new field data. It does not generalize, reject, or blame; those are stronger moves than the text supports.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A claim the text has not supported
questions.learningObjective: Spot an unsupported claim in a brief
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asserts 'This material will outlast the competition's by a decade,' with no test data. Why is that claim unsupported?

answer.exemplar: The claim predicts long-term durability without any accelerated aging, field, or comparative test data, so nothing in the brief supports the decade advantage.

questions.explanation: A durability prediction needs evidence of testing or comparison; absent that, it is an assertion. The tempting reading treats confidence of tone as proof.
questions.hint: Look for test data backing the decade claim.

stimulus.body: Our team prefers the new tool. Therefore every engineer will prefer it.

questions.stem: Which claim in the brief is unsupported?

options.text: 'Our team prefers the new tool.'
options.misconception: treats the stated preference as unsupported

options.text: 'Every engineer will prefer it.'
Both claims are unsupported.
options.misconception: groups the supported preference with the overreach

options.text: Neither claim is unsupported.

questions.explanation: The team's preference is stated; extending it to every engineer is an unsupported generalization. The two claims differ in support.
questions.hint: Compare the two subjects: team vs every engineer.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: Find the main idea in a recommendation
questions.stem: A brief recommends replacing a pump and spends most of its space on failure rates. What is the main idea?

answer.exemplar: The main idea is that the pump should be replaced, supported by evidence of its failure rates.

questions.explanation: The recommendation is the point; failure rates are the support. Treating failure rates as the main idea inverts the structure.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.stem: Stage one: a brief says 'Maximum current: 5 A.' Stage two: what is the maximum current?

options.text: 10 A, doubling the value.
5 V, confusing current with voltage.
5 A, as stated.
No limit is given.

questions.explanation: The brief states 5 A. Voltage, doubled values, or absence are not in the text.
questions.hint: Read the number with its unit.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.stem: Which sentence from a brief sounds most skeptical?

options.text: 'The vendor is our valued partner.'
'The vendor guarantees perfect results.'
'We fully trust the vendor's data.'
'The vendor's claims seem optimistic and need verification.'

questions.explanation: 'Seem optimistic and need verification' expresses doubt. Guarantee, trust, and partnership signal the opposite.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Attitude and the evidence offered for it

stimulus.body: The seal kept water out during a 30-minute immersion test. The design team calls the seal 'reliable.'

questions.stem: Is the evidence adequate for the attitude 'reliable'?

options.text: No, because reliability requires only cost data.
Yes, because immersion testing supports water reliability.
No, because one test is never enough.
Yes, because 'reliable' means only appearance.

questions.explanation: A water-immersion test directly supports water reliability. Cost-only or appearance-only readings misdefine the term.
questions.hint: Match the test to the claim's dimension.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Purpose and how a writer signals it
questions.stem: A brief states 'Do not exceed 80 degrees or damage will occur.' What purpose does that sentence serve?

answer.exemplar: The sentence warns of a damage threshold, aiming to prevent misuse of the product.

questions.explanation: A conditional warning about damage is preventive, not informational or persuasive in the usual sense. Missing the warning reads it as a spec.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.stem: Stage one: a brief says 'Because the gasket hardened, the seal failed.' Stage two: what move is that?

options.text: A comparison of two gaskets.
options.misconception: reads a single case as a comparison

options.text: A definition of a gasket.
options.misconception: confuses a causal claim with a definition

options.text: A cause-effect claim linking hardening to failure.
A prediction about future gaskets.
options.misconception: reads a past cause as a forecast

questions.explanation: 'Because' plus a result states cause and effect. It is not definitional, comparative, or predictive.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A claim the text has not supported
questions.stem: A brief says 'We should switch suppliers,' with no comparison of suppliers. What is unsupported?

options.text: Nothing; recommendations need no evidence.
The existence of suppliers.
options.misconception: treats a background fact as unsupported

options.text: The need for any supplier.
options.misconception: misreads the claim as denying suppliers

options.text: The recommendation to switch suppliers.

questions.explanation: A switch recommendation needs comparative evidence; absent that, it is unsupported. The existence of suppliers is not in question.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: Find the main idea in a conclusion

stimulus.body: After reviewing all options, the team concludes that safety overrides cost. Cost remains a constraint, not the goal.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of this brief excerpt?

options.text: Cost is the primary goal.
Safety overrides cost.
The team reviewed all options.
options.misconception: treats a process note as the main idea

options.text: Cost is no longer a constraint.

questions.explanation: The conclusion states safety overrides cost; reviewing options is process and cost remains a constraint. The main idea is the priority claim.

questions.stem: A brief specifies 'RAL 9005 jet black.' What detail is given?

answer.exemplar: The detail is the color standard and shade: RAL 9005, jet black.

questions.explanation: RAL 9005 names a standard color; 'jet black' describes it. Reading only 'black' loses the specification.
questions.hint: Note the standard code and shade name.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.stem: Stage one: a brief says 'We regret the delay and are sorry for the inconvenience.' Stage two: what tone is that?

Proud and celebratory.
Apologetic and regretful.
Demanding and impatient.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Attitude and the evidence offered for it
questions.stem: A brief calls a bracket 'overengineered' and cites a safety factor of 4. Is that evidence adequate?

options.text: Yes, because overengineered means underdesigned.
No, because safety factors are never relevant.
No, because 4 is too small to matter.
Yes, a safety factor of 4 suggests excess margin.

questions.explanation: A safety factor of 4 indicates substantial excess margin, supporting 'overengineered.' The term means excess, not deficiency.

questions.topic: Purpose and how a writer signals it

questions.stem: What purpose do these sentences serve?

options.text: To argue against heavy designs.
To define key terms for the brief.
To list test procedures.
To set the project budget.

questions.explanation: 'Means' signals definitions. They are not arguments, test lists, or budgets.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.stem: An engineer writes 'Fasteners fail in three ways: shear, tension, and fatigue.' What move is that?

answer.exemplar: The engineer exemplifies the failure modes, listing three concrete types to illustrate the category.

questions.explanation: Listing concrete instances illustrates a category, an exemplification move. It is not a definition or a contrast.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A claim the text has not supported
questions.stem: Stage one: a brief predicts 'Sales will triple.' Stage two: what is missing?

options.text: A list of current employees.
The product's color.
Market data or growth drivers.
Nothing; predictions need no support.

questions.explanation: A sales prediction needs market evidence; color or employee lists do not establish growth, and predictions are never self-evident.
questions.hint: Ask what supports a number about the future.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: Identify the main idea of a spec
questions.stem: A spec's first line is 'This device must be waterproof.' Later lines list color and price. What is the main idea?

options.text: All three are equally main ideas.
Color is the primary concern.
Price drives the design.
The device must be waterproof.

questions.explanation: The first line states the governing requirement; color and price are secondary. They do not share equal status.

stimulus.body: The finished unit weighs 1.2 kg including battery. Packaging adds 0.3 kg.

questions.stem: What is the unit's weight including battery?

1.2 kg, as stated.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.stem: A brief states 'This design will outperform every competitor, guaranteed.' What tone is that?

answer.exemplar: The tone is highly confident and assertive, using 'will' and 'guaranteed' to project certainty.

questions.explanation: 'Will' and 'guaranteed' project certainty. A hedged or neutral tone would use 'may' or bare specifications.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Attitude and the evidence offered for it
questions.stem: Stage one: a brief calls a coating 'durable' and cites a 500-hour salt-spray test. Stage two: is the evidence adequate?

options.text: No, because 500 hours is too short.
No, because durability means only color retention.
Yes, because salt-spray testing supports corrosion durability.
Yes, because any test proves everything.
options.misconception: overstates what a single test shows

questions.explanation: A salt-spray test directly addresses corrosion durability, so the evidence is adequate for that dimension. It does not prove every aspect of durability, but it does support the claim.
questions.hint: Match the test to the claim's dimension.
